questions.q: In the Request-Reply pattern's checkout/tax example, why must the callout happen before any DML that depends on the result?
options: Because Request-Reply always runs asynchronously
Because Flow cannot make callouts at all
Because a transaction can't make a callout while it has pending uncommitted DML, so the tax callout must resolve before saving anything that depends on it
Because tax calculation APIs never return a usable result
questions.explain: This directly applies the transaction-ordering rule from Lesson 7 — the synchronous callout must complete before the dependent DML, not after.

questions.q: What is the specific risk this lesson identifies with the Fire and Forget pattern if misapplied?
options: It cannot be implemented with Queueable Apex
It requires a WSDL document to function
It always exceeds the 100-callouts-per-transaction limit
Because the caller doesn't wait for or inspect a detailed result, a Fire and Forget call can silently fail unnoticed unless result-checking or a callback is built in
questions.explain: "Fire and forget" should never mean "fire and never find out" — unmonitored fire-and-forget calls risk silent failure.

questions.q: Why is Batch Apex, rather than a single synchronous transaction, the right implementation for Batch Data Synchronization at scale?
options: Because each Batch Apex execute chunk gets its own fresh governor limits, suited to volumes too large to process in one synchronous transaction
Because Batch Apex doesn't require a Named Credential
Because synchronous Apex cannot perform SOQL queries
Because Batch Apex is faster per record than synchronous Apex
questions.explain: Batch Apex's scoped-chunk execution gives each chunk fresh governor limits, which is exactly why it fits large volumes that a single transaction couldn't handle.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the risk of misapplying Batch Data Synchronization to a requirement that actually needs near-instant consistency?
options: There is no risk — Batch Sync is always appropriate
Batch Sync's nightly or hourly cadence produces stale, wrong answers exactly when near-real-time accuracy matters most, such as checkout inventory checks
Batch Sync will exceed the 120-second cumulative callout timeout
Batch Sync cannot be scheduled on a recurring basis
questions.explain: Batch Sync trades real-time accuracy for throughput; a requirement needing near-instant consistency is a sign it's actually Request-Reply or event-driven instead.

questions.q: Which wording cue does this lesson associate with the Fire and Forget pattern?
options: "immediately update the screen"
"before," "needs the result to," or "can't proceed without"
"notify," "kick off," or "doesn't need to wait"
"nightly," "reconcile," or "in bulk"
questions.explain: Wording like "notify," "kick off," or "doesn't need to wait" signals a Fire and Forget requirement, as opposed to Request-Reply's "before"/"needs the result" cues or Batch Sync's "nightly"/"in bulk" cues.
